en: The Apadāna of the Elder Dhammasavaṇiya Gandhodaka Chapter, Number 9 I was a monk in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, And I was known as Dhammasavaṇiya. I went to hear the Dhamma from the Teacher, And having heard it, I rejoiced in it with a glad heart. Having passed away from there, I was reborn in heaven; There I enjoyed the fivefold sense-pleasures. After enjoying celestial bliss for a long time, I was reborn here in the human world. In this world, I am now a monk endowed with wisdom; I have attained the fruit of Arhatship. By the power of that merit, I have reached the goal; I have transcended birth and death, and am free from all suffering. Thus did the Elder Dhammasavaṇiya speak of his own past deeds.
“The Victor named Padumuttara,
who had gone beyond all phenomena,
was proclaiming the Four Noble Truths.”
He delivered many people across.
At that time,
I was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities.
Shaking off my bark garments,
I then went through the air above the Best of Buddhas.
I am not able to go;
like a bird striking against a rock,
I find no way to proceed.
Never before has this disturbance of my posture occurred,
as if one had emerged from the water.
Thus I travel through the sky.
Having become sublime, I shall remain seated below that man.
Come now, I shall search for it;
perhaps I may find the goal.
Descending from the sky,
I heard the sound of the Teacher as he was speaking of impermanence;
at that time, I grasped it.
Having grasped the perception of impermanence,
I went to my own hermitage;
having lived there for as long as my life lasted, I passed away.
There, having passed away,
as my final existence was unfolding,
I remembered that hearing of the Dhamma.
By that well-performed deed,
I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for thirty thousand eons.
I took delight in the world of the gods,
and for fifty-one times,
I exercised sovereignty over the devas.
And seventy-one times I was a wheel-turning monarch;
I also held extensive regional sovereignty.
Incalculable by number;
having sat in his father’s house,
the ascetic with developed faculties—
Explaining by means of a verse,
he proclaimed impermanence:
"I remember that perception."
Wandering through various states of existence,
I did not penetrate the limit—
the deathless state of Nibbāna.
Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena,
subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease.
The subsiding of these is bliss.
Having heard the verse,
I recollected my former karma.
Sitting upon a single seat,
I attained arahantship;
I was only seven years old by birth.
I attained arahantship;
the Buddha, the Seer, granted me full ordination, recognizing my virtues.
Being but a young girl,
I have completed my task; what remains for me to do today?
In the teaching of the Son of the Sakyan,
a hundred thousand aeons ago,
that deed which I performed at that time—
I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit of hearing the true Dhamma.
The four analytical knowledges—
the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
Thus indeed did the Venerable Elder Dhammasavaniya speak these verses.
The legend of the Elder Dhammasavaniya is the ninth.
